cases.question: Tell me about Mercury.
cases.reference_answer: 'Mercury' commonly refers to the planet (closest to the Sun), the chemical element Hg, or the Roman god.
cases.expected_behavior: Answer the most likely sense (e.g. the planet) fully and cite it, then briefly note the other senses (element, Roman god).

answer.text:
"Mercury" is one of the most versatile names in science, history, and mythology. Here are the three most common meanings:

---

MERCURY THE PLANET

Mercury is the first planet from the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System. It is a rocky world with a surface that closely resembles Earth's Moon, covered in craters and bright ray systems. Its largest crater, Caloris Planitia, is about 1,550 km (960 mi) across — roughly one-third of the planet's diameter of 4,880 km (3,030 mi).

Mercury completes one orbit around the Sun every 88 Earth days, but its solar day (sunrise to sunrise) lasts about 176 Earth days because of its unusual 3:2 spin-orbit resonance. Temperatures on its surface swing dramatically, from -170 °C (-270 °F) at night to 420 °C (790 °F) in direct sunlight. Despite this, its permanently shadowed polar craters may contain water ice. Mercury has a very thin exosphere and a weak magnetic field. It was first visited by the Mariner 10 spacecraft in 1974, and later explored by the MESSENGER and BepiColombo orbiters.

---

MERCURY THE ELEMENT

Mercury (chemical symbol Hg, atomic number 80) is a chemical element also commonly known as quicksilver. It is unique among metals in being the only one that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure. It is a heavy, silvery substance that occurs naturally mostly as cinnabar (mercuric sulfide), from which the red pigment vermilion is derived.

Mercury has been used in thermometers, barometers, fluorescent lamps, and other devices. However, it is highly toxic — exposure harms the nervous system, immune system, and kidneys in humans and animals — so its use in everyday products has been greatly reduced over time.

---

MERCURY THE ROMAN GOD

In Roman religion and mythology, Mercury (Latin: Mercurius) is one of the 12 major gods of the Roman pantheon. He is the god of commerce, communication, luck, travelers, and thieves, and also serves as the guide of souls to the underworld. He is the son of Jupiter and Maia (daughter of the Titan Atlas), and is closely equivalent to the Greek god Hermes. Mercury is traditionally depicted holding the caduceus, a staff with intertwined snakes.

---

The planet and element are both named after the Roman god. There are also many other things named Mercury, including companies, newspapers, music, and more.

Sources:
Mercury (planet) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet)
Mercury (element) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element)
Mercury (mythology) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(mythology)

cases.question: If all roses are flowers and some flowers fade quickly, can we conclude that all roses fade quickly?
cases.reference_answer: No — that conclusion does not follow logically.
cases.expected_behavior: Answer the reasoning directly without searching; note it is not from Wikipedia.

answer.text:
This is a question of logical reasoning, not a factual lookup, so I can answer it directly without consulting Wikipedia.

No, we cannot conclude that all roses fade quickly. Here is why:

The argument presented is a classic example of a logical fallacy known as the "undistributed middle" or an invalid syllogism. Let's break it down:

Premise 1: All roses are flowers. (Every rose belongs to the set of flowers.)
Premise 2: Some flowers fade quickly. (Only a part of the set of flowers fades quickly.)
Conclusion: Therefore, all roses fade quickly. (INVALID)

The flaw lies in Premise 2. It only tells us that some flowers fade quickly, not all of them. Since roses are a subset of flowers, they could fall into either the "fades quickly" group or the "does not fade quickly" group. We simply do not have enough information to place all roses into the "fades quickly" category.

To illustrate with a clear example: imagine flowers are divided into daisies (which fade quickly) and roses (which do not fade quickly). Both premises would still be true, yet the conclusion "all roses fade quickly" would be false.

For the conclusion to be valid, Premise 2 would need to say "All flowers fade quickly." Only then could we logically chain the two premises together to conclude that all roses fade quickly.

In summary, the argument is logically invalid. The two premises, as stated, do not support the conclusion.

Here is what Wikipedia says about Pushpavanam village:

Pushpavanam is a village located in the Vedaranyam subdistrict of Nagapattinam District in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu. It sits on the coast of the Bay of Bengal, about 10.3 km north of Vedaranyam taluk, 34.8 km south of Nagapattinam, and approximately 291 km from Chennai. It is effectively situated on an island, bordered by the Vedaranyam Canal (Uppanar River) to the southwest and the Vettar River to the north.

cases.question: What is the best programming language?
cases.expected_behavior: Explain there is no single factual 'best' (it depends on use case); do not assert an opinion as fact. Answer without searching and note Wikipedia has no factual answer.
cases.notes: Subjective abstention: real-sounding question with no factual answer.

answer.text:
This is a matter of opinion and context, not a factual question, so this answer does not come from Wikipedia — it reflects general knowledge about the topic.

There is no single "best" programming language. The right choice depends on what you are trying to do, your experience level, and your goals. Here are some common use cases and popular languages for each:

Web Development: JavaScript is essentially unavoidable for front-end work, while Python, Ruby, PHP, and Node.js are popular on the back end.

Data Science and Machine Learning: Python is the dominant choice, thanks to libraries like NumPy, Pandas, and TensorFlow. R is also widely used for statistics.

Systems Programming and Performance: C, C++, and Rust are top choices when speed and low-level control matter.

Mobile Development: Swift is the standard for iOS, while Kotlin is preferred for Android. Dart (with Flutter) allows cross-platform mobile development.

General Purpose and Beginners: Python is widely recommended for beginners due to its clean, readable syntax. Java is also a classic choice taught in many universities.

Enterprise Software: Java and C# have long dominated enterprise environments.

Game Development: C++ and C# (with the Unity engine) are most common.

In short, no language wins in every situation. Python is often cited as the most versatile and beginner-friendly, and JavaScript as the most universally present (especially on the web), but the "best" language is always the one that best fits your specific needs and project requirements.
